options.rationale: This child has fulminant macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) complicating sJIA, evidenced by the paradoxical fall in ESR and WCC (from previously high levels), massively elevated ferritin (above 10,000 microg/L), falling fibrinogen (DIC), encephalopathy, cytopenias, and organ dysfunction. First-line treatment is high-dose IV methylprednisolone (30 mg/kg, max 1 g, daily for 3 days) followed by oral dexamethasone. Cyclosporin A is added as second-line or concurrently in severe cases. ICU admission is essential for haemodynamic monitoring and management of coagulopathy. Anakinra dose escalation may be added. (Source: PRINTO/PRES: MAS Classification Criteria; ACR/EULAR sJIA-MAS Treatment Recommendations)

options.text: Fresh frozen plasma and platelet transfusion with observation
options.rationale: Blood product support (FFP, cryoprecipitate for fibrinogen, platelets) is important supportive care for the consumptive coagulopathy, but does not address the underlying immune dysregulation driving MAS. Without immunosuppressive treatment, the cytokine storm will continue consuming blood products. Observation without immunosuppression risks rapid deterioration and death. (Source: PRINTO/PRES: MAS Classification Criteria)

options.text: Etoposide-based chemotherapy per HLH-2004 protocol
options.rationale: The HLH-2004 protocol (etoposide, dexamethasone, cyclosporin) is used for primary (genetic) haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. MAS complicating sJIA is a secondary form that typically responds to corticosteroids and cyclosporin without the need for etoposide. Etoposide is reserved for refractory MAS not responding to first-line immunosuppression. (Source: ACR/EULAR sJIA-MAS Treatment Recommendations)

explanation.summary: Macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) is a life-threatening complication of systemic JIA, occurring in 10-15% of sJIA patients. It is characterised by uncontrolled macrophage and T-cell activation with a cytokine storm. The key diagnostic clues are paradoxical changes: falling ESR (from fibrinogen consumption), falling WCC and platelets (from previously elevated levels in sJIA), and massively rising ferritin. MAS shares criteria with secondary haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH). Treatment is high-dose corticosteroids with cyclosporin as second-line. Mortality without treatment approaches 20-30%.
key_points: Paradoxically falling ESR in active sJIA is a red flag for MAS (ESR falls because fibrinogen is consumed)
Ferritin above 10,000 microg/L in sJIA is highly suggestive of MAS
Falling WCC and platelets FROM previously elevated levels (not just low counts) is characteristic
First-line: IV methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg (max 1 g) daily for 3 days; second-line: cyclosporin A
Anakinra dose escalation (up to 10 mg/kg/day) is increasingly used as adjunctive therapy in sJIA-MAS
explanation.pearls: The most specific early warning sign of MAS in sJIA is a paradoxical fall in ESR while ferritin rises - this discordance occurs because fibrinogen (the main determinant of ESR) is consumed by DIC while ferritin is released by activated macrophages.

stem: A 14-month-old boy presents with a 3-month history of developmental regression. He had been walking with support but has lost this skill and now has truncal hypotonia and can no longer sit unsupported. His parents describe episodic vomiting and lethargy, often during minor illnesses. He was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy. Family history reveals a maternal uncle who died at age 3 from an undiagnosed neurological condition.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 130, RR 28, SpO2 98%, Temp 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Truncal hypotonia with appendicular spasticity. Nystagmus. Absent deep tendon reflexes. Intermittent dystonic posturing of the upper limbs. Growth parameters: weight 9.2 kg (10th centile, was 25th), length 75 cm (25th centile).
data_table.Investigations: Venous lactate 5.8 mmol/L (elevated). Pyruvate 0.08 mmol/L. Lactate-to-pyruvate ratio 72 (elevated, normal < 20). Plasma alanine elevated. CSF lactate 4.2 mmol/L (elevated, normal < 2.0 mmol/L). Urine organic acids: elevated lactate and Krebs cycle intermediates.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the suspected diagnosis?

options.text: Whole exome sequencing including mitochondrial DNA analysis
options.rationale: Genetic testing is the ultimate confirmatory investigation for mitochondrial disease but requires targeted analysis informed by the clinical and imaging phenotype. While whole exome sequencing will eventually be performed, MRI brain should be obtained first as the characteristic Leigh syndrome pattern (bilateral symmetric basal ganglia and brainstem lesions) narrows the differential and guides genetic testing priorities. (Source: RCPCH: Mitochondrial Disease; GeneReviews: Leigh Syndrome)

options.text: Muscle biopsy with respiratory chain enzyme analysis
options.rationale: Muscle biopsy with mitochondrial respiratory chain enzyme analysis was historically the gold standard for diagnosing mitochondrial disorders. However, it is invasive, may show normal results in some mitochondrial diseases (especially mtDNA mutations with tissue mosaicism), and has been largely superseded by genetic testing as the primary diagnostic tool. It remains useful when genetic testing is inconclusive. (Source: RCPCH: Mitochondrial Disease)

options.text: Skin fibroblast culture for respiratory chain enzyme assay
options.rationale: Fibroblast culture is less invasive than muscle biopsy but requires 4-6 weeks for cell growth and has lower sensitivity than muscle tissue. It is not the first-line investigation for a child with a classic clinical presentation and biochemical profile. Imaging should precede invasive tissue testing. (Source: GeneReviews: Leigh Syndrome)

options.text: Electroencephalogram with prolonged monitoring for epilepsy
options.rationale: While seizures occur in mitochondrial disease, EEG is not the diagnostic investigation. This child's presentation is one of developmental regression with movement disorder and metabolic derangement, not primarily epilepsy. EEG may be useful for seizure characterisation but does not confirm the underlying mitochondrial diagnosis. (Source: RCPCH: Mitochondrial Disease)

options.text: MRI brain with spectroscopy for characteristic lesion pattern
options.rationale: MRI brain is the most appropriate next investigation. Leigh syndrome characteristically shows bilateral symmetric T2-hyperintense lesions in the basal ganglia (putamen and caudate), thalami, and brainstem (periaqueductal grey, substantia nigra). MR spectroscopy may show an elevated lactate peak within the lesions. This pattern, combined with the clinical features (developmental regression, movement disorder, nystagmus), elevated blood and CSF lactate with a high lactate-to-pyruvate ratio, and maternal inheritance pattern, makes a clinical diagnosis of Leigh syndrome. The imaging pattern guides subsequent genetic testing. (Source: RCPCH: Mitochondrial Disease; GeneReviews: Leigh Syndrome)

explanation.summary: Leigh syndrome (subacute necrotising encephalomyelopathy) is the most common paediatric mitochondrial disorder, caused by defects in mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. It presents with developmental regression, movement disorders, and brainstem dysfunction in infancy or early childhood. The hallmark is bilateral symmetric basal ganglia and brainstem lesions on MRI. The elevated lactate-to-pyruvate ratio above 20 indicates impaired oxidative phosphorylation. Maternal inheritance (through a maternal uncle) suggests a mitochondrial DNA mutation. Over 75 nuclear and mitochondrial genes have been implicated. There is no curative treatment; management is supportive with cofactor supplementation.
key_points: Leigh syndrome shows bilateral symmetric T2-hyperintense lesions in the basal ganglia and brainstem on MRI
Elevated lactate-to-pyruvate ratio above 20 indicates impaired mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation
CSF lactate is often elevated even when blood lactate is normal, reflecting CNS metabolic dysfunction
Maternal inheritance pattern suggests mitochondrial DNA mutation (maternally inherited through mothers to all children)
Episodic metabolic decompensation during intercurrent illness is characteristic of mitochondrial disease
explanation.pearls: In Leigh syndrome, the lactate-to-pyruvate ratio above 20 distinguishes mitochondrial respiratory chain defects (elevated ratio) from pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency (normal or low ratio) - both cause lactic acidosis and basal ganglia lesions, but the treatment implications differ (ketogenic diet for PDH deficiency, cofactor supplementation for respiratory chain defects).

subtopic_detail: Inborn errors of metabolism - neonatal presentation
stem: A 5-day-old term neonate born via uncomplicated vaginal delivery is brought to the emergency department with poor feeding, vomiting, and progressive lethargy over the past 24 hours. The parents are first cousins. The newborn screening results are not yet available. The neonate is hypotonic with a weak cry. There is no rash, fontanelle is flat, and there are no dysmorphic features.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 170, RR 55, SpO2 96% RA, Temp 36.4, Weight 3.2 kg
data_table.Investigations: VBG: pH 7.18, pCO2 22 mmHg, HCO3 10 mmol/L, lactate 5.2 mmol/L, anion gap 24 mmol/L; BSL 3.8 mmol/L; ammonia 680 micromol/L (ref <50); FBC: WCC 11.2, Hb 165 g/L, platelets 220; CRP <1 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management step?

options.text: Cease enteral feeds and commence IV 10% dextrose infusion
options.rationale: In suspected urea cycle defects or organic acidaemias presenting with hyperammonaemia, the immediate priority is to halt protein catabolism by ceasing enteral feeds (the protein source) and providing high-rate IV dextrose to suppress catabolism and provide energy substrate. This buys time while awaiting specialist metabolic input and definitive investigations. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyperammonaemia)

options.text: Administer IV sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg as a slow bolus
options.rationale: Sodium bicarbonate corrects the acidosis symptomatically but does not address the underlying cause of hyperammonaemia. Ammonia continues to rise if protein catabolism is not halted. Bicarbonate may also cause paradoxical CNS acidosis and sodium load. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyperammonaemia)

options.text: Start IV ceftriaxone and obtain blood cultures urgently
options.rationale: Neonatal sepsis is a reasonable differential for an unwell neonate, and empiric antibiotics may be given alongside metabolic management. However, the markedly elevated ammonia (680 micromol/L) with a normal CRP, consanguinity, and high anion gap acidosis point strongly to a metabolic disorder. Antibiotics do not address the ammonia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange urgent haemodialysis for ammonia clearance
options.rationale: Haemodialysis is the most effective method of ammonia removal and is indicated when ammonia exceeds approximately 400-500 micromol/L depending on trajectory. However, it requires specialist setup and is not the initial management step - cessation of protein and IV glucose must begin immediately while dialysis is being arranged. (Source: JIMD Reports)

options.text: Commence oral sodium benzoate as an ammonia scavenger
options.rationale: Sodium benzoate is an ammonia scavenger used in urea cycle defects, but it is given IV (not orally) in acute decompensation, and it is a secondary intervention after the immediate step of stopping protein intake and providing glucose. Oral administration in a vomiting neonate is also impractical. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyperammonaemia)

explanation.summary: Neonatal hyperammonaemia is a metabolic emergency. The most common causes include urea cycle defects and organic acidaemias. The immediate management priority is to halt catabolism by ceasing protein-containing feeds and providing high-rate IV glucose. Definitive ammonia clearance via haemodialysis should be arranged in parallel when ammonia exceeds 400-500 micromol/L, but the first action is always metabolic stabilisation. Consanguinity raises the pre-test probability of autosomal recessive metabolic disorders.
key_points: Hyperammonaemia >200 micromol/L in a neonate is a metabolic emergency requiring immediate intervention
Cease all protein intake and provide IV 10% dextrose at 1.5x maintenance to suppress catabolism
Haemodialysis is the most efficient ammonia removal method but requires specialist setup
Normal CRP and absence of risk factors for sepsis shift the differential towards inborn errors of metabolism
Newborn screening may not detect all urea cycle defects and results may not yet be available at day 5
explanation.pearls: Ammonia levels above 400 micromol/L in neonates warrant haemodialysis referral, but the first bedside action is always cessation of protein plus IV dextrose - this can be done within minutes while organising dialysis access.

stem: A 14-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department after an 8-minute episode of left-sided rhythmic jerking associated with a fever of 39.2 degrees Celsius. The seizure was terminated with buccal midazolam by paramedics. She has been previously well with no developmental concerns and immunisations are up to date. On arrival she is drowsy but rousable to voice. The fontanelle is flat and soft. There is no neck stiffness, rash, or focal neurological deficit on examination. Tympanic membranes are dull bilaterally.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 155, RR 32, SpO2 98% RA, Temp 38.8 (post-midazolam)
data_table.Investigations: BSL 5.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Discharge home with written febrile seizure safety advice
options.rationale: Discharge would be appropriate for a simple febrile seizure in a child over 12 months. However, this seizure is complex (focal, lasting >15 minutes equivalent with the 8-minute duration plus time to termination). In a child under 18 months with complex features, further investigation including LP consideration is warranted before discharge. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Seizure)

options.text: Perform a lumbar puncture once the child is more alert
options.rationale: This child has a complex febrile seizure (focal, prolonged) at age 14 months. In children under 18 months with complex febrile seizures, the threshold for LP should be low because meningism is unreliable at this age. The flat fontanelle and absence of raised ICP signs make LP safe. Waiting until the child is more alert is appropriate post-ictal management. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Seizure)

options.text: Commence IV levetiracetam for seizure prophylaxis now
options.rationale: Antiepileptic prophylaxis is not indicated after febrile seizures, even complex ones. Febrile seizures do not constitute epilepsy and long-term antiepileptics carry side-effect risk that outweighs the modest recurrence reduction. Intermittent oral diazepam during febrile illnesses may be discussed for frequent recurrences. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Seizure)

options.text: Arrange an urgent CT brain before any further workup
options.rationale: CT brain is not routinely indicated for febrile seizures, even complex ones, unless there are signs of raised intracranial pressure, persistent focal deficit, or clinical suspicion of an intracranial pathology. This child has a flat fontanelle and no focal signs post-ictally. CT would delay more important investigations. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Seizure)

options.text: Request an EEG within the next 24 hours for assessment
options.rationale: EEG is not recommended acutely after febrile seizures. Post-ictal EEG findings are non-specific and do not reliably predict epilepsy risk. EEG may be considered if there are recurrent complex febrile seizures or afebrile seizures subsequently, but it is not part of the acute assessment. (Source: NICE CG176: Fever in Under 5s)

explanation.summary: Complex febrile seizures are defined by focal features, duration greater than 15 minutes, or recurrence within 24 hours. In children under 18 months, signs of meningitis are unreliable, so the threshold for lumbar puncture should be low when complex features are present. The bilateral dull tympanic membranes suggest otitis media as the fever source, but this does not exclude concurrent meningitis. Neuroimaging and EEG are not part of routine febrile seizure workup.
key_points: Complex febrile seizure features: focal, >15 min duration, recurrence within 24 hours, or post-ictal focal deficit
LP threshold is low in children <18 months with complex febrile seizures because meningism is unreliable
Antiepileptic prophylaxis is not indicated for febrile seizures
CT brain is only indicated if signs of raised ICP or persistent focal deficit
EEG is not useful in the acute febrile seizure setting
explanation.pearls: In children under 18 months with complex febrile seizures, perform LP even when the fontanelle is flat and there is no neck stiffness - meningeal signs are unreliable below this age and meningitis must be actively excluded.

stem: An 8-year-old girl is referred to the paediatric outpatient clinic by her teacher, who reports multiple daily episodes of staring blankly for 5 to 10 seconds, during which she does not respond. The episodes have been occurring for three months and are increasing in frequency. Her mother reports occasional eyelid fluttering during the episodes. She is otherwise developmentally normal and has no history of tonic-clonic seizures. There is no significant medical or family history. An EEG shows 3 Hz generalised spike-and-wave discharges provoked by hyperventilation.

data_table.Examination: Neurological examination normal, no dysmorphic features, growth on 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line antiepileptic drug?

options.text: Carbamazepine 5 mg/kg/day in two divided doses orally
options.rationale: Carbamazepine is contraindicated in absence epilepsy as it can worsen absence seizures and may precipitate absence status epilepticus. It acts on sodium channels and is ineffective against the thalamocortical T-type calcium channel mechanism underlying absences. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Sodium valproate 10 mg/kg/day in two divided doses orally
options.rationale: Sodium valproate is effective for absence epilepsy and was historically first-line. However, in girls and women of childbearing potential, valproate carries significant teratogenic risk and should be avoided as first-line where alternatives exist. Australian and international guidelines now recommend ethosuximide for pure absence epilepsy in females. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Ethosuximide 10 mg/kg/day in two divided doses orally
options.rationale: Ethosuximide is first-line for childhood absence epilepsy, particularly in females given the teratogenicity concerns with valproate. It specifically targets T-type calcium channels in the thalamocortical circuit responsible for absence seizures. The SANAD II trial confirmed equivalent efficacy to valproate for absence epilepsy with a better side-effect profile. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Lamotrigine 0.5 mg/kg/day with slow titration upwards
options.rationale: Lamotrigine is a reasonable second-line option for absence epilepsy and avoids valproate teratogenicity concerns. However, it is less effective than ethosuximide for absence seizures as monotherapy and requires very slow titration over weeks to months due to the risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome, making it unsuitable as first choice. (Source: ILAE Treatment Guidelines)

options.text: Levetiracetam 10 mg/kg/day in two divided doses orally
options.rationale: Levetiracetam is broadly used in paediatric epilepsy but has limited evidence for absence seizures specifically. It is not recommended as first-line for childhood absence epilepsy by Australian or ILAE guidelines. Its mechanism does not target the T-type calcium channels involved in absence seizure generation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Childhood absence epilepsy is characterised by frequent brief absence seizures with 3 Hz spike-and-wave on EEG. Ethosuximide is first-line, particularly in females, as it avoids valproate teratogenicity while maintaining equivalent efficacy. Sodium valproate remains an option if generalised tonic-clonic seizures coexist but should be avoided in girls where possible. Carbamazepine and phenytoin are contraindicated as they worsen absences. The prognosis is good, with approximately 70% of children achieving remission by adolescence.
key_points: Ethosuximide is first-line for childhood absence epilepsy, especially in females
Carbamazepine is contraindicated in absence epilepsy and can worsen seizures
Valproate is effective but avoided first-line in females due to teratogenicity
3 Hz generalised spike-and-wave on EEG provoked by hyperventilation is the classic finding
Lamotrigine is second-line but requires slow titration and is less effective for absences
explanation.pearls: Carbamazepine and phenytoin - both sodium channel blockers - can paradoxically worsen absence epilepsy and even trigger absence status epilepticus; always confirm the epilepsy syndrome before prescribing.

stem: A 6-year-old boy with known systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis on methotrexate and prednisolone presents with three days of worsening fever to 40 degrees Celsius, increasing lethargy, and a new petechial rash. His JIA had been in remission for 6 months. On arrival she is afebrile and her left hip examination is unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 165, BP 85/50 mmHg, RR 34, SpO2 95% RA, Temp 40.1
data_table.Investigations: FBC: Hb 92 g/L, WCC 2.1 x10^9/L, platelets 42 x10^9/L; ESR 8 mm/hr (previously 65); CRP 180 mg/L; ferritin 18,400 microg/L; fibrinogen 0.8 g/L (ref 2.0-4.0); triglycerides 4.8 mmol/L; ALT 285 U/L; AST 420 U/L; LDH 1,850 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Increase the methotrexate dose to achieve disease control
options.rationale: Methotrexate is a disease-modifying agent for JIA maintenance but is ineffective for acute macrophage activation syndrome (MAS). It also suppresses bone marrow and could worsen the cytopenias. MAS is an emergency requiring rapid immunosuppression with different agents. (Source: RCH CPG: Macrophage Activation Syndrome)

options.text: Commence IV ceftriaxone and vancomycin for presumed sepsis
options.rationale: The presentation overlaps with severe sepsis - fever, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly, coagulopathy. However, the paradoxically falling ESR (8, previously 65) with rising CRP, massively elevated ferritin (>10,000), low fibrinogen, and hypertriglyceridaemia in a child with sJIA are diagnostic of MAS. Antibiotics alone do not treat the underlying hyperinflammatory state. (Source: RCH CPG: Macrophage Activation Syndrome)

options.text: Commence urgent plasmapheresis for cytokine clearance
options.rationale: Plasmapheresis may be considered as a rescue therapy in refractory MAS or haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH), but it is not the initial treatment. First-line therapy for MAS complicating sJIA is high-dose corticosteroids, with ciclosporin added if refractory. Plasmapheresis requires central access and specialist support. (Source: Histiocyte Society HLH-2004 Protocol)

options.text: Administer high-dose IV etoposide as per HLH protocol
options.rationale: Etoposide-based HLH protocols (HLH-94/2004) are used for primary HLH and refractory secondary HLH. MAS complicating sJIA typically responds well to high-dose corticosteroids and ciclosporin, and etoposide carries significant toxicity including myelosuppression. It would only be considered if first-line MAS treatment fails. (Source: Histiocyte Society HLH-2004 Protocol)

options.text: Commence IV methylprednisolone pulse therapy 30 mg/kg/day
options.rationale: High-dose IV methylprednisolone (pulse dosing up to 30 mg/kg/day, max 1 g) is the first-line treatment for MAS complicating sJIA. The falling ESR with rising CRP and ferritin is a hallmark of MAS - the ESR falls because fibrinogen (an acute phase reactant and ESR determinant) is consumed by the coagulopathy. Ciclosporin is added if there is no response within 24-48 hours. (Source: RCH CPG: Macrophage Activation Syndrome)

explanation.summary: Macrophage activation syndrome is a life-threatening complication of systemic JIA, representing a form of secondary haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. The diagnostic hallmark is a paradoxically falling ESR (due to fibrinogen consumption) with markedly rising ferritin, in the context of cytopenias, hepatic dysfunction, and coagulopathy. First-line treatment is high-dose IV corticosteroids, with ciclosporin added for refractory cases. The HLH-2004 etoposide-based protocol is reserved for primary HLH or MAS not responding to steroids and ciclosporin.
key_points: Falling ESR with rising CRP and ferritin is the hallmark of MAS - ESR drops because fibrinogen is consumed
Ferritin above 10,000 microg/L in a child with sJIA should trigger immediate investigation for MAS
First-line treatment is IV methylprednisolone pulse therapy
Ciclosporin is second-line for steroid-refractory MAS
MAS can be triggered by infections, medication changes, or disease flares in sJIA
explanation.pearls: A falling ESR in a child with sJIA who is clinically deteriorating is a red flag for MAS - the ESR drops because fibrinogen is being consumed by disseminated intravascular coagulation, not because the disease is improving.

stem: A 4-month-old male infant is brought to the emergency department by his father who reports the baby 'rolled off the couch' approximately two hours ago. The infant is irritable and holds his right arm still. There are no bruises visible. Examination reveals swelling and tenderness of the right mid-humerus. X-ray shows a spiral fracture of the right humeral shaft. The father appears anxious and provides inconsistent accounts of the mechanism when asked again by the nurse.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 160, RR 38, SpO2 99% RA, Temp 36.9
data_table.Investigations: X-ray right humerus: spiral mid-shaft fracture with no periosteal reaction; no other injuries visible on this film

lead_in: What is the most important next step?

options.text: Make a mandatory notification to child protection services
options.rationale: A spiral humeral fracture in a pre-mobile 4-month-old infant with an inconsistent and implausible mechanism (4-month-olds cannot roll off couches with enough force for a spiral humeral fracture) raises a high index of suspicion for non-accidental injury. All Australian states and territories have mandatory reporting legislation requiring notification. A skeletal survey and further workup should follow, but notification must not be delayed. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

options.text: Apply a splint and arrange orthopaedic follow-up this week
options.rationale: Fracture management is necessary but does not address the child protection concern. Treating the fracture and discharging the infant without notification places the child at risk of further harm. Orthopaedic management occurs in parallel with child protection assessment, not instead of it. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

options.text: Request a skeletal survey before considering notification
options.rationale: A skeletal survey is an important part of the non-accidental injury workup and may reveal occult fractures of different ages. However, waiting for the skeletal survey before notifying child protection is inappropriate - notification should occur as soon as reasonable suspicion exists, and a spiral fracture in a pre-mobile infant with inconsistent history meets that threshold. (Source: NSW Health: Mandatory Reporting)

options.text: Obtain coagulation studies and calcium to exclude pathology
options.rationale: Metabolic bone disease (e.g. osteogenesis imperfecta) and coagulopathy should be considered in the differential for unexplained fractures. However, these are uncommon and do not negate the obligation to notify child protection when the clinical picture is suspicious. Investigation for organic causes and child protection notification should occur in parallel. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

options.text: Admit for observation and request social work consultation
options.rationale: Admission and social work involvement are appropriate adjuncts but are not substitutes for mandatory notification to the statutory child protection authority. Social workers can support the family and assist with the process, but the doctor has a legal obligation to notify directly. Delaying notification pending social work review risks the child's safety. (Source: NSW Health: Mandatory Reporting)

explanation.summary: Spiral fractures in pre-mobile infants are highly suspicious for non-accidental injury, particularly when the reported mechanism is inconsistent or biomechanically implausible. A 4-month-old cannot generate the rotational force required for a spiral humeral fracture by rolling off a couch. Mandatory reporting is a legal obligation for doctors across all Australian jurisdictions when there is reasonable suspicion of abuse. Investigation for organic causes (skeletal survey, bloods) and fracture treatment proceed in parallel with child protection involvement.
key_points: Spiral long-bone fractures in pre-mobile infants are highly suspicious for non-accidental injury
Mandatory notification to child protection occurs as soon as reasonable suspicion exists
A skeletal survey should be performed but notification should not wait for results
Inconsistent or biomechanically implausible mechanisms raise the index of suspicion
Investigation for organic causes (osteogenesis imperfecta, metabolic bone disease) occurs in parallel with notification
explanation.pearls: The humeral shaft is the most common long-bone fracture site in physical child abuse in infants under 12 months - a spiral or oblique pattern in a pre-mobile child has a positive predictive value for abuse exceeding 80%.

stem: A 3-year-old boy presents with a 24-hour history of refusal to bear weight on his left leg. He had an upper respiratory tract infection five days ago that has resolved. He is febrile at 38.9 degrees Celsius. Examination shows the left hip held in flexion and external rotation with marked pain on attempted internal rotation. He screams when the hip is passively moved. He is able to bear weight briefly on the right leg only.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 140, RR 28, SpO2 98% RA, Temp 38.9, Weight 15 kg
data_table.Investigations: FBC: WCC 16.8 x10^9/L, neutrophils 12.4; CRP 78 mg/L; ESR 42 mm/hr; hip ultrasound: moderate left hip joint effusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Prescribe oral ibuprofen and reassess in 24 to 48 hours
options.rationale: This approach would be appropriate for transient synovitis, which typically follows viral illness in a well-looking child with low-grade or absent fever and normal inflammatory markers. This child has fever above 38.5, elevated CRP and WCC, and inability to bear weight - features that satisfy Kocher criteria for a high probability of septic arthritis. (Source: RCH CPG: Limping Child)

options.text: Perform urgent ultrasound-guided hip joint aspiration
options.rationale: This child meets 3 of 4 Kocher criteria (fever >38.5, non-weight-bearing, WCC >12, ESR >40), giving a predicted probability of septic arthritis exceeding 90%. Joint aspiration is essential to confirm the diagnosis, identify the organism, and guide antibiotic therapy. The effusion confirmed on ultrasound makes aspiration technically feasible. (Source: RCH CPG: Limping Child)

options.text: Commence IV flucloxacillin empirically without aspiration
options.rationale: Empiric antibiotics are necessary for septic arthritis but should ideally be given after joint aspiration to maximise the chance of identifying the causative organism. Starting antibiotics before obtaining synovial fluid reduces culture yield and may lead to prolonged empiric therapy. Aspiration also serves a therapeutic role by decompressing the joint. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange MRI of the left hip to clarify the diagnosis first
options.rationale: MRI can demonstrate joint effusion, synovial enhancement, and adjacent osteomyelitis, but it takes time to arrange, requires sedation in a 3-year-old, and delays definitive management. Ultrasound has already confirmed an effusion. Aspiration is both diagnostic and therapeutic and should not be delayed for MRI when the clinical picture is clear. (Source: RCH CPG: Limping Child)

options.text: Obtain a plain X-ray of the left hip and pelvis urgently
options.rationale: Plain X-ray is part of the initial workup for a limping child and can exclude fracture or bony pathology. However, X-ray is insensitive for early septic arthritis - it may show soft tissue swelling or widened joint space but cannot distinguish septic arthritis from transient synovitis. Ultrasound has already demonstrated the effusion. Aspiration is the priority. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Septic Arthritis)

explanation.summary: The Kocher criteria help distinguish septic arthritis from transient synovitis in children presenting with hip pain and effusion. The four criteria are: fever above 38.5, non-weight-bearing, WCC above 12 x10^9/L, and ESR above 40 mm/hr. With 3 or 4 criteria met, the probability of septic arthritis exceeds 90% and urgent joint aspiration is indicated. Staphylococcus aureus is the most common organism in this age group. Antibiotics should be withheld until after aspiration when possible, but not delayed if aspiration is impractical.
key_points: Kocher criteria: fever >38.5, non-weight-bearing, WCC >12, ESR >40 - three or more predicts >90% probability of septic arthritis
Joint aspiration is both diagnostic and therapeutic and should precede antibiotics when feasible
Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of septic arthritis in children
Transient synovitis typically follows viral illness but presents with lower or absent fever and normal inflammatory markers
CRP above 20 mg/L is a useful additional predictor (Caird modification of Kocher criteria)
explanation.pearls: Adding CRP above 20 mg/L to the original Kocher criteria (the Caird modification) improves specificity - a child meeting 4 of 5 modified criteria has a predicted probability of septic arthritis exceeding 98%.

stem: A 12-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with a 3-week history of worsening left knee pain. He has a BMI of 32 kg/m2. He walks with an antalgic gait favouring the left side. On examination, the left knee has a full range of movement without effusion. When the left hip is flexed, it obligately externally rotates. Internal rotation of the left hip is limited to 10 degrees and reproduces his knee pain. The right hip examination is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, BP 110/68 mmHg, Temp 36.7
data_table.Examination: Left knee: no swelling, no tenderness, full ROM; Left hip: obligate external rotation on flexion, internal rotation 10 degrees (right 40 degrees), pain with log roll

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial investigation?

options.text: X-ray of the left knee in two views as the pain localises there
options.rationale: Knee pain in a child or adolescent with an unremarkable knee examination should prompt assessment of the hip, as referred pain from hip pathology is common via the obturator nerve. The normal knee examination and abnormal hip findings indicate the pathology is in the hip. An isolated knee X-ray would miss the diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Limping Child)

options.text: Bilateral hip X-ray including anteroposterior and frog-leg lateral
options.rationale: The clinical picture - obese adolescent male with insidious onset knee pain, obligate external rotation of the hip on flexion, and limited internal rotation - is classic for slipped upper femoral epiphysis (SUFE). Bilateral hip X-rays including frog-leg lateral views are essential, as the slip is often seen on the lateral view (Trethowan sign) and up to 40% of cases have bilateral involvement. (Source: RCH CPG: Limping Child)

options.text: MRI of the left hip to assess for avascular necrosis early
options.rationale: MRI is sensitive for early SUFE and avascular necrosis but is not the initial investigation. Plain X-ray will confirm the diagnosis in most cases and is faster, cheaper, and does not require sedation. MRI may be indicated if X-ray is inconclusive in a pre-slip or early SUFE. (Source: POSNA: SCFE)

options.text: Ultrasound of the left hip to evaluate for a joint effusion
options.rationale: Hip ultrasound is useful for detecting effusion in younger children where transient synovitis or septic arthritis is suspected. In an afebrile obese 12-year-old with insidious onset symptoms and obligate external rotation, SUFE is far more likely than an inflammatory or infective process. Plain X-ray is the appropriate first-line investigation. (Source: RCH CPG: Limping Child)

options.text: Blood tests including FBC, CRP, and ESR to exclude infection
options.rationale: Inflammatory markers are useful when septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, or inflammatory arthritis is suspected. This child is afebrile with a chronic insidious history and classic mechanical signs of SUFE. Blood tests would not contribute to the diagnosis and could delay appropriate imaging. (Source: RCH CPG: Limping Child)

explanation.summary: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis is a common hip disorder of adolescence where the femoral head displaces posteriorly and inferiorly relative to the neck through the growth plate. Classic risk factors include obesity and male sex. The hallmark examination finding is obligate external rotation of the hip on flexion, with limited internal rotation. Knee pain is a common presenting complaint due to referred pain via the obturator nerve. Bilateral X-rays are essential as bilateral involvement occurs in up to 40% of cases.
key_points: Obligate external rotation on hip flexion with limited internal rotation is the hallmark of SUFE
Knee pain with normal knee examination in an adolescent should prompt hip examination
Bilateral AP and frog-leg lateral hip X-rays are the initial investigation of choice
Risk factors include obesity, male sex, adolescence, and endocrine disorders (hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency)
Up to 40% of SUFE cases have bilateral involvement - always image both hips
explanation.pearls: The frog-leg lateral view reveals early SUFE before it becomes visible on AP X-ray - Klein's line drawn along the superior femoral neck should intersect the lateral epiphysis; failure to do so (positive Trethowan sign) confirms the slip.

stem: A 13-year-old girl with a BMI of 34 kg/m2 presents to the emergency department unable to weight-bear on her right leg after tripping on a step one hour ago. She reports two weeks of intermittent right groin aching prior to the fall. On examination, the right leg lies shortened and externally rotated. Any attempt to internally rotate or flex the hip causes severe pain. She is afebrile and her left hip examination is unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 105, BP 108/66 mmHg, Temp 36.6, SpO2 99% RA
data_table.Investigations: AP pelvis X-ray: widened right proximal femoral physis with posterior displacement of the right femoral epiphysis; left hip normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Allow protected weight-bearing and arrange outpatient review
options.rationale: This is an acute-on-chronic unstable SUFE - the patient cannot weight-bear. Unstable SUFE carries a high risk of avascular necrosis of the femoral head (up to 47%), and any further displacement must be prevented. Weight-bearing is contraindicated and urgent surgical fixation is required. (Source: RCH CPG: SUFE)

options.text: Commence traction and arrange semi-urgent orthopaedic review
options.rationale: Traction was historically used for SUFE but is no longer recommended as it does not prevent further displacement and may delay definitive fixation. Current guidelines recommend bed rest with no manipulation and urgent orthopaedic consultation for in-situ fixation within 24 hours. (Source: POSNA: SCFE)

options.text: Arrange urgent closed reduction under general anaesthesia today
options.rationale: Forced reduction of SUFE increases the risk of avascular necrosis by disrupting the remaining blood supply to the femoral head through the retinacular vessels. Current practice favours gentle in-situ fixation with a single cannulated screw rather than attempting to restore anatomy through reduction. (Source: RCH CPG: SUFE)

options.text: Keep non-weight-bearing and arrange urgent in-situ screw fixation
options.rationale: This is an acute-on-chronic unstable SUFE based on the inability to weight-bear, pre-existing symptoms, and radiographic findings. Management is strict non-weight-bearing (bed rest, stretcher transport) and urgent in-situ fixation with a single cannulated screw to prevent further displacement. The aim is to stabilise the epiphysis in its current position, not to reduce it. (Source: RCH CPG: SUFE)

options.text: Request MRI to assess femoral head vascularity before surgery
options.rationale: MRI can assess femoral head perfusion and predict avascular necrosis risk, but it should not delay urgent surgical fixation. Each hour of delay increases the risk of further displacement and vascular compromise. MRI may be obtained post-fixation if avascular necrosis is suspected clinically. (Source: POSNA: SCFE)

explanation.summary: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis is classified as stable (able to weight-bear) or unstable (unable to weight-bear). Unstable SUFE carries a significantly higher rate of avascular necrosis (up to 47% vs 0-5% for stable). The treatment for both is in-situ fixation with a cannulated screw, but unstable SUFE requires urgent fixation. Reduction is avoided as it increases avascular necrosis risk. The contralateral hip should be monitored as prophylactic pinning is controversial but discussed in high-risk patients.
key_points: Unstable SUFE is defined by inability to weight-bear and carries up to 47% risk of avascular necrosis
Treatment is urgent in-situ screw fixation without reduction
Forced reduction increases avascular necrosis risk by disrupting retinacular blood supply
Traction is no longer recommended for SUFE management
Risk factors include obesity, endocrine disorders, and adolescence during the growth spurt
explanation.pearls: The Loder classification distinguishes stable (can weight-bear, even with crutches) from unstable (cannot weight-bear at all) SUFE - this single clinical distinction predicts avascular necrosis risk better than the degree of radiographic slip.

stem: An 11-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department after a generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 3 minutes at home. He has had gastroenteritis with vomiting and reduced oral intake for 36 hours. He was born at term with no neonatal complications. His newborn screening was reportedly normal. He has had two previous hospital presentations with hypoglycaemia during intercurrent illness at ages 4 and 8 months, both attributed to 'fasting intolerance' and managed with IV dextrose. On arrival he is drowsy and postictal.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 170, RR 40, SpO2 97% RA, Temp 37.2, Weight 9.5 kg
data_table.Investigations: BSL 1.2 mmol/L; VBG: pH 7.28, HCO3 18 mmol/L, lactate 2.8 mmol/L; urinary ketones: trace; FBC and UEC normal; LFTs: ALT 95 U/L, AST 110 U/L

lead_in: What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?

options.text: Ketotic hypoglycaemia of childhood triggered by fasting
options.rationale: Ketotic hypoglycaemia is the most common cause of hypoglycaemia in children aged 18 months to 5 years and characteristically presents with marked ketonuria during fasting. This child has hypoketotic hypoglycaemia (trace urinary ketones despite BSL 1.2), which is inconsistent with ketotic hypoglycaemia and suggests a fatty acid oxidation disorder. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Congenital hyperinsulinism with recurrent fasting episodes
options.rationale: Congenital hyperinsulinism causes hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, which fits the biochemical picture. However, it typically presents in the neonatal period with persistent hypoglycaemia requiring high glucose infusion rates. Presentation at 11 months triggered specifically by fasting during illness, with normal inter-illness intervals, is more consistent with a fatty acid oxidation defect. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Growth hormone deficiency causing recurrent hypoglycaemia
options.rationale: Growth hormone deficiency can cause fasting hypoglycaemia in children, but it is typically accompanied by ketosis (as fat is mobilised but glucose production is impaired). The hypoketotic pattern and mildly elevated transaminases in this child point towards a fatty acid oxidation disorder rather than a hormone deficiency. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Adrenal insufficiency with cortisol deficiency during stress
options.rationale: Adrenal insufficiency can cause hypoglycaemia during physiological stress, but like growth hormone deficiency, it is associated with ketotic hypoglycaemia rather than hypoketotic. Additionally, electrolyte disturbances (hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia) would be expected in primary adrenal insufficiency, and the UEC is normal. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (MCADD)
options.rationale: MCADD is the most common fatty acid oxidation disorder and presents with hypoketotic hypoglycaemia during periods of fasting or metabolic stress. The hallmark is inappropriately low ketones for the degree of hypoglycaemia, mildly elevated transaminases from hepatic fat accumulation, and recurrent episodes triggered by intercurrent illness. Newborn screening detects most but not all cases. The history of recurrent fasting hypoglycaemia with trace ketones is classic. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

explanation.summary: MCADD is an autosomal recessive disorder of mitochondrial fatty acid beta-oxidation affecting approximately 1 in 10,000 live births. During fasting, the body cannot adequately oxidise medium-chain fatty acids for energy, leading to hypoketotic hypoglycaemia. The cardinal biochemical finding is inappropriately low ketones for the degree of hypoglycaemia. Newborn screening via tandem mass spectrometry detects elevated octanoylcarnitine (C8), but false negatives occur. Treatment is avoidance of prolonged fasting and emergency IV dextrose during illness.
key_points: Hypoketotic hypoglycaemia (low BSL with inappropriately low ketones) suggests a fatty acid oxidation disorder
MCADD is the most common fatty acid oxidation disorder, detectable on newborn screening
Presentation is typically during fasting stress from intercurrent illness in infancy or early childhood
Mild hepatic transaminase elevation occurs due to fatty infiltration during metabolic decompensation
Newborn screening is not 100% sensitive - clinical suspicion should prompt confirmatory acylcarnitine profile and genetic testing
explanation.pearls: The critical distinction is ketotic vs hypoketotic hypoglycaemia - when BSL is below 2.6 mmol/L, urinary ketones should be at least 2+ if fat oxidation pathways are intact; trace or absent ketones with severe hypoglycaemia mandates investigation for MCADD or hyperinsulinism.

stem: A 4-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department with a 2-day history of widespread petechiae and bruising on her limbs and trunk. She had a viral upper respiratory tract infection two weeks ago that has fully resolved. She is well-appearing, afebrile, and active. There is no hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. She has no bleeding from mucosal surfaces.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 100, BP 95/60 mmHg, Temp 36.8, SpO2 99% RA
data_table.Investigations: FBC: Hb 125 g/L, WCC 7.2 x10^9/L (normal differential), platelets 8 x10^9/L; blood film: reduced platelets, no blasts, normal red cell morphology; coagulation studies normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Observation with activity restriction and close follow-up
options.rationale: This child has newly diagnosed immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) with skin-only bleeding (petechiae, bruising) and no mucosal haemorrhage. Despite the very low platelet count, current Australian and international guidelines recommend observation with activity restriction for ITP with skin-only manifestations, as spontaneous resolution occurs in approximately 80% of childhood ITP within 6 months. Treatment is reserved for significant mucosal bleeding. (Source: RCH CPG: ITP)

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day for five to seven days
options.rationale: Oral prednisolone accelerates platelet recovery and is indicated in ITP with significant mucosal bleeding (epistaxis, gingival bleeding, haematuria) or when quality of life is significantly impaired. For skin-only manifestations in a well child, the side effects of corticosteroids (mood disturbance, weight gain, immunosuppression) outweigh the benefits. (Source: RCH CPG: ITP)

options.text: Administer intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg as a single dose
options.rationale: IVIG provides the fastest platelet rise (typically within 24-48 hours) and is indicated in ITP with life-threatening bleeding, significant mucosal haemorrhage, or when an urgent procedure is required. It is not first-line for skin-only ITP due to cost, infusion reactions, and the benign natural history of the condition. (Source: HSANZ: ITP Guidelines)

options.text: Transfuse one unit of pooled platelets to reduce bleeding risk
options.rationale: Platelet transfusion is generally avoided in ITP as the transfused platelets are rapidly destroyed by the same autoimmune mechanism. Platelet transfusion is reserved for life-threatening haemorrhage (intracranial, gastrointestinal) where temporising measures are needed. In skin-only ITP, platelet transfusion is not indicated. (Source: RCH CPG: ITP)

options.text: Perform a bone marrow aspirate to exclude acute leukaemia
options.rationale: Bone marrow aspirate is not routinely required in typical childhood ITP presenting with isolated thrombocytopenia, normal white cell count and differential, and no hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. The blood film shows no blasts. Bone marrow aspirate is indicated if corticosteroids are to be commenced (to exclude leukaemia mimicking ITP) or if atypical features are present. (Source: RCH CPG: ITP)

explanation.summary: Childhood ITP is an autoimmune condition causing isolated thrombocytopenia, typically following a viral illness. The platelet count alone does not dictate treatment - management is guided by bleeding severity. Skin-only manifestations (petechiae, bruising) without mucosal bleeding are managed with observation and activity restriction. Approximately 80% of childhood ITP resolves spontaneously within 6 months. Pharmacological treatment is reserved for significant mucosal bleeding, and IVIG is used for life-threatening haemorrhage.
key_points: ITP management is guided by bleeding severity, not platelet count alone
Skin-only ITP in a well child is managed with observation and activity restriction
Corticosteroids are reserved for significant mucosal bleeding in ITP
IVIG provides the fastest platelet rise and is used for severe or life-threatening bleeding
Platelet transfusion is generally ineffective in ITP due to autoimmune destruction
explanation.pearls: In childhood ITP, a platelet count of 8 x10^9/L with skin-only bleeding is managed with observation alone - the decision to treat is based on the severity of bleeding, not the number on the blood count.

stem: A 9-month-old boy presents with 6 days of fever up to 39.5 degrees Celsius that has not responded to paracetamol or ibuprofen. He has bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, cracked erythematous lips, and irritability. He does not have a rash, cervical lymphadenopathy, or limb changes. All cultures and viral studies are negative. Urinalysis shows sterile pyuria.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 165, RR 36, SpO2 98% RA, Temp 39.3
data_table.Investigations: FBC: WCC 18.2 x10^9/L, Hb 98 g/L, platelets 480 x10^9/L; CRP 125 mg/L; ESR 72 mm/hr; ALT 65 U/L; albumin 26 g/L; urinalysis: WCC 15/hpf, no growth on culture; blood cultures negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue supportive care and reassess in 24 to 48 hours
options.rationale: This child has 6 days of fever with 2 of 5 classic Kawasaki criteria (conjunctival injection, lip changes), meeting the definition of incomplete Kawasaki disease. Infants under 12 months are at highest risk of coronary artery aneurysms and incomplete presentations are more common in this age group. Delaying treatment increases the risk of coronary involvement. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Commence high-dose aspirin and arrange outpatient echocardiography
options.rationale: Aspirin is part of Kawasaki management but is given alongside IVIG, not alone. Furthermore, echocardiography should be performed urgently (not as an outpatient) given the 6 days of fever and high risk of coronary involvement in an infant. Aspirin monotherapy is insufficient to prevent coronary artery aneurysms. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Request urgent echocardiography and administer IVIG 2 g/kg
options.rationale: This infant meets criteria for incomplete Kawasaki disease: fever for 5 or more days with 2-3 classic features, plus supportive laboratory findings (CRP >30, ESR >40, albumin <30, anaemia, thrombocytosis, elevated ALT, sterile pyuria). In infants under 12 months with incomplete Kawasaki, the threshold for treatment should be low due to higher coronary risk. IVIG 2 g/kg over 10-12 hours plus high-dose aspirin is the standard treatment. Echocardiography assesses coronary arteries. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Start empiric IV antibiotics for possible occult bacterial focus
options.rationale: Blood and urine cultures are negative, and the sterile pyuria is characteristic of Kawasaki disease rather than urinary tract infection. The clinical picture with prolonged fever, conjunctival injection, lip changes, and supportive laboratories is more consistent with Kawasaki disease than occult bacterial infection. Antibiotics would not prevent coronary artery aneurysms. (Source: AHA Kawasaki Disease Guidelines)

options.text: Obtain a CT angiogram of the coronary arteries for assessment
options.rationale: CT angiography is not the initial cardiac investigation in suspected Kawasaki disease. Transthoracic echocardiography is the standard imaging modality for assessing coronary artery dimensions in children. CT carries radiation exposure and typically requires sedation. It may be used later for detailed follow-up of known aneurysms. (Source: AHA Kawasaki Disease Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Incomplete Kawasaki disease is defined by fever for 5 or more days with fewer than 4 of the 5 classic clinical criteria, supported by laboratory abnormalities. It is more common in infants under 12 months, who are paradoxically at highest risk of coronary artery aneurysms. The laboratory features supporting the diagnosis include CRP above 30 mg/L, ESR above 40 mm/hr, hypoalbuminaemia, anaemia, thrombocytosis, elevated transaminases, and sterile pyuria. Treatment with IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin should not be delayed.
key_points: Incomplete Kawasaki: fever >=5 days with 2-3 classic criteria plus supportive lab findings
Infants under 12 months have the highest risk of coronary aneurysms and most commonly present incompletely
IVIG 2 g/kg as a single infusion over 10-12 hours is the standard treatment
Sterile pyuria is a supportive laboratory finding for Kawasaki disease
Treatment within 10 days of fever onset reduces coronary aneurysm risk from 25% to approximately 4%
explanation.pearls: Sterile pyuria in Kawasaki disease results from urethral inflammation causing white cells in urine that is culture-negative - it occurs in up to 80% of cases and should not be mistaken for UTI.

stem:
A 16-day-old male infant born at term is brought to the emergency department with poor feeding, vomiting, and lethargy over the past 3 days. The parents report increasing drowsiness and two episodes of dusky spells. The newborn screening result collected on day 3 has not yet been returned. On examination, the infant is dehydrated with mottled skin, delayed capillary refill of 4 seconds, and appears shocked.

The external genitalia appear normal male with bilaterally descended testes. There is hyperpigmentation of the scrotum and nipples noted by the parents as present from birth.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 185, RR 60, SpO2 92% RA, Temp 36.2, Weight 3.0 kg (birth weight 3.4 kg)
data_table.Investigations: BSL 1.8 mmol/L; VBG: pH 7.22, pCO2 28 mmHg, HCO3 12 mmol/L, K+ 7.8 mmol/L, Na+ 118 mmol/L; FBC: Hb 180 g/L, WCC 14.2, platelets 310

lead_in: What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?

options.text: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia with salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase deficiency
options.rationale: This male neonate presents in salt-wasting adrenal crisis at day 16 - the classic timing for 21-hydroxylase deficiency. The combination of hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, metabolic acidosis, and shock is pathognomonic for mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid deficiency. Hyperpigmentation from ACTH excess supports the diagnosis. Male infants with classic CAH have normal genitalia, so the diagnosis is often missed until salt-wasting crisis at 1-3 weeks of life. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia)

options.text: Late-onset neonatal sepsis with secondary adrenal suppression
options.rationale: Neonatal sepsis can cause shock with electrolyte derangement, but the specific pattern of hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia is more consistent with primary adrenal insufficiency than sepsis-related adrenal suppression. Sepsis typically causes hyponatraemia without hyperkalaemia, and the hyperpigmentation present from birth suggests a congenital rather than acquired process. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia)

options.text: Pyloric stenosis with secondary dehydration and electrolyte loss
options.rationale: Pyloric stenosis presents with projectile vomiting at 2-6 weeks of age but causes hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis from gastric acid loss - the opposite electrolyte pattern to this case. This infant has metabolic acidosis with hyperkalaemia, which is inconsistent with pyloric stenosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

options.text: Congenital renal tubular acidosis with potassium retention
options.rationale: Type 4 renal tubular acidosis can cause hyperkalaemic metabolic acidosis, but it does not explain the severe hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia, or shock in this presentation. The combination of all four features (hypoNa, hyperK, hypo BSL, shock) at day 16 of life with hyperpigmentation is far more consistent with congenital adrenal hyperplasia. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia)

options.text: Congenital heart disease with cardiogenic shock and end-organ failure
options.rationale: Duct-dependent congenital heart disease can present with shock in the first weeks of life as the ductus arteriosus closes. However, it does not cause the specific electrolyte pattern of hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia. Cardiogenic shock would typically present with hepatomegaly, tachypnoea, and differential saturations rather than this metabolic picture. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease)

explanation.summary: Classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency is the most common cause of congenital adrenal hyperplasia, accounting for over 90% of cases. Salt-wasting forms present at 1-3 weeks of life with adrenal crisis characterised by hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, metabolic acidosis, and circulatory collapse. Female infants are typically diagnosed earlier due to virilised genitalia at birth, but male infants have normal external genitalia and are often only diagnosed at salt-wasting crisis. Newborn screening detects elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone but results may not be available before presentation.
key_points: Salt-wasting CAH typically presents at 1-3 weeks of life as mineralocorticoid reserves are depleted
Male infants with CAH have normal external genitalia and are diagnosed later than females
The electrolyte triad of hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, and hypoglycaemia with metabolic acidosis is characteristic
Hyperpigmentation from ACTH excess may be present from birth
Emergency treatment is IV 0.9% NaCl, IV dextrose, and IV hydrocortisone 25 mg bolus
explanation.pearls: Male infants with salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase deficiency present on average 5-7 days later than females because their normal external genitalia do not trigger earlier investigation - the salt-wasting crisis at day 10-21 is often the first clinical clue.

stem: A 10-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents who are concerned about episodic inconsolable crying and pallor. The episodes last 2 to 3 minutes and occur every 15 to 20 minutes. Between episodes the infant appears lethargic but is not distressed. He had a viral gastroenteritis one week ago that resolved. He has had one loose stool with a red-tinged mucoid appearance. On examination the abdomen is soft between episodes but the infant draws up his knees and screams during an observed episode.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 150, RR 34, SpO2 98% RA, Temp 37.0
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft between episodes, no distension, no palpable mass, red-tinged mucoid stool on nappy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Plain abdominal X-ray in supine and erect views urgently
options.rationale: Plain abdominal X-ray has poor sensitivity (approximately 50%) for intussusception. It may show a soft tissue mass, meniscus sign, or absent caecal gas, but a normal X-ray does not exclude the diagnosis. Ultrasound is the investigation of choice with sensitivity exceeding 98%. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast for detailed assessment
options.rationale: CT is not the first-line investigation for suspected intussusception in a paediatric patient. It involves significant radiation exposure and typically requires sedation in an infant. Abdominal ultrasound provides superior diagnostic accuracy for intussusception without radiation. CT may be used if complications are suspected (e.g. perforation). (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Abdominal ultrasound to evaluate for a target or doughnut sign
options.rationale: Abdominal ultrasound is the gold-standard investigation for intussusception with sensitivity of 98-100% and specificity of 88-100%. The classic finding is the target sign (or doughnut sign) on transverse view, representing the layers of intussuscepted bowel. This child has a classic presentation: episodic colicky pain with drawing up of knees, inter-episode lethargy, and red currant jelly stool. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Proceed directly to therapeutic air enema without prior imaging
options.rationale: Air enema is both diagnostic and therapeutic for ileocolic intussusception and has a reduction success rate of approximately 80-95%. However, it should be preceded by ultrasound confirmation to avoid unnecessary intervention. Air enema also carries risks of perforation and should be performed by an experienced radiologist with surgical standby. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Obtain stool cultures and viral PCR to identify the causative agent
options.rationale: The preceding viral gastroenteritis is a common antecedent to intussusception (via mesenteric lymphoid hyperplasia acting as a lead point), but identifying the specific virus does not change management. The priority is diagnosing and treating the intussusception, not characterising the preceding infection. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Intussusception)

explanation.summary: Intussusception is the most common cause of bowel obstruction in infants aged 3 months to 3 years. The classic triad of colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, and red currant jelly stool is present in only 20-40% of cases. Inter-episode lethargy is an important and often underappreciated feature. Abdominal ultrasound is the investigation of choice with near-perfect sensitivity. Treatment is air or hydrostatic enema reduction, with surgical intervention reserved for failed reduction or perforation.
key_points: Abdominal ultrasound has sensitivity >98% for intussusception and is the first-line investigation
The classic triad (colicky pain, vomiting, red currant jelly stool) is present in only 20-40% of cases
Inter-episode lethargy or pallor may be the dominant feature and should raise suspicion
Air enema reduction has a success rate of 80-95% for ileocolic intussusception
Preceding viral illness is a common trigger via mesenteric lymphoid hyperplasia
explanation.pearls: Inter-episode lethargy in an infant with episodic distress is a red flag for intussusception - up to 30% of cases present with altered consciousness as the dominant feature, sometimes without obvious abdominal pain.

stem: A 10-year-old boy with no prior medical history presents to the emergency department with a 3-week history of polyuria, polydipsia, and 4 kg weight loss. He is now vomiting and has Kussmaul breathing. He is alert and oriented. His weight is 32 kg. He has been given a 10 mL/kg 0.9% NaCl bolus for mild dehydration. His blood glucose is 28 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 120, BP 100/65 mmHg, RR 32 (deep), SpO2 99% RA, Temp 36.9, GCS 15
data_table.Investigations: VBG: pH 7.12, pCO2 18 mmHg, HCO3 8 mmol/L, K+ 5.2 mmol/L; BSL 28 mmol/L; ketones (blood) 5.8 mmol/L; Na+ 131 mmol/L (corrected Na+ 137); UEC: creatinine 65 micromol/L

lead_in: After the initial bolus, what is the most appropriate fluid and insulin strategy?

options.text: 0.9% NaCl at 5 mL/kg/hr with insulin at 0.1 unit/kg/hr started after 1 hour of fluids
options.rationale: A fluid rate of 5 mL/kg/hr is excessive for paediatric DKA and increases the risk of cerebral oedema. Australian guidelines (ISPAD/RCH) recommend calculating total fluid replacement over 48 hours using maintenance plus deficit (estimated at 5-7% dehydration), with deficit replaced evenly over 48 hours. Insulin at 0.1 unit/kg/hr is correct. (Source: RCH CPG: DKA)

options.text: 0.9% NaCl at maintenance plus 5% deficit over 48 hours, insulin at 0.05 unit/kg/hr after 1 hour
options.rationale: This fluid strategy is close to correct but the insulin dose of 0.05 unit/kg/hr is below the standard starting rate. ISPAD guidelines recommend starting at 0.1 unit/kg/hr for paediatric DKA. A rate of 0.05 unit/kg/hr may be used for younger children or if blood glucose falls too rapidly, but it is not the standard starting dose. (Source: RCH CPG: DKA)

options.text: 0.9% NaCl at maintenance plus 5% deficit over 48 hours, insulin at 0.1 unit/kg/hr after 1 hour
options.rationale: This follows Australian and ISPAD paediatric DKA guidelines. Fluid is calculated as maintenance plus estimated deficit (5% for moderate DKA based on pH 7.12 and clinical assessment) replaced evenly over 48 hours. Insulin infusion at 0.1 unit/kg/hr is commenced 1 hour after starting IV fluids to avoid rapid osmotic shifts. The slower rehydration over 48 hours reduces the risk of cerebral oedema compared to more aggressive regimens. (Source: RCH CPG: DKA)

options.text: 0.45% NaCl at maintenance rate with insulin at 0.1 unit/kg/hr started immediately after bolus
options.rationale: Hypotonic fluids (0.45% NaCl) should not be used in the initial phase of paediatric DKA management as they can exacerbate cerebral oedema by increasing the osmotic gradient. Isotonic 0.9% NaCl is used initially. Additionally, starting insulin immediately after the bolus without the recommended 1-hour fluid-first period may cause rapid glucose and osmolality shifts. (Source: RCH CPG: DKA)

options.text: 0.9% NaCl at maintenance plus 7% deficit over 24 hours, insulin at 0.1 unit/kg/hr after 1 hour
options.rationale: Replacing the deficit over 24 hours rather than 48 hours is too rapid for paediatric DKA. Rapid fluid administration increases the risk of cerebral oedema, which is the leading cause of DKA-related mortality in children. Australian and ISPAD guidelines specifically recommend deficit replacement over 48 hours. (Source: ISPAD DKA Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Paediatric DKA fluid management differs significantly from adult protocols due to the risk of cerebral oedema. Fluid deficit is estimated at 5% for moderate and 7% for severe DKA and is replaced evenly over 48 hours using isotonic saline. Insulin infusion at 0.1 unit/kg/hr is commenced 1 hour after starting IV fluids. Blood glucose should not fall faster than 5 mmol/L/hr. When BSL reaches 15-17 mmol/L, glucose is added to the fluid to allow continued insulin infusion for ketone clearance.
key_points: Paediatric DKA fluid deficit is replaced over 48 hours to reduce cerebral oedema risk
0.9% NaCl is used initially - not hypotonic fluids
Insulin at 0.1 unit/kg/hr is started 1 hour after commencing IV fluids
Blood glucose target fall rate is no more than 5 mmol/L/hr
Add 5% dextrose to IV fluids when BSL reaches 15-17 mmol/L to allow continued insulin for ketone clearance
explanation.pearls: The corrected sodium should rise as blood glucose falls during DKA treatment - a falling corrected sodium is a warning sign for developing cerebral oedema and warrants immediate reassessment of fluid rate and consideration of hypertonic saline or mannitol.

stem: A 3-year-old girl presents with a 5-day history of bloody diarrhoea followed by 2 days of decreasing urine output and pallor. She attended a petting zoo one week before symptom onset. On examination she is pale with periorbital oedema. She has not received any antibiotics during this illness. Stool culture has returned positive for Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli O157:H7.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 130, BP 108/72 mmHg (above 95th centile), RR 28, Temp 37.1
data_table.Investigations: FBC: Hb 72 g/L, WCC 14.8 x10^9/L, platelets 38 x10^9/L; blood film: schistocytes present, helmet cells; UEC: creatinine 280 micromol/L (baseline ~30), urea 22 mmol/L, K+ 5.9 mmol/L, Na+ 132 mmol/L; LDH 2,400 U/L; haptoglobin <0.1 g/L; reticulocyte count elevated

lead_in: Which of the following interventions should be specifically avoided?

options.text: Platelet transfusion to correct the severe thrombocytopenia
options.rationale: Platelet transfusion is relatively contraindicated in typical HUS as it may fuel the thrombotic microangiopathy by providing substrate for further microvascular thrombosis. However, it may be given for active life-threatening bleeding or before invasive procedures. While it should be avoided if possible, it is not the most specifically contraindicated intervention. (Source: RCH CPG: HUS)

options.text: Packed red cell transfusion to maintain haemoglobin above 70 g/L
options.rationale: Red cell transfusion is appropriate and recommended in HUS when haemoglobin falls below 60-70 g/L or the patient is symptomatic. Unlike platelet transfusion, packed red cells do not contribute to the thrombotic microangiopathy. Transfusion should be given slowly to avoid fluid overload in the setting of renal failure. (Source: RCH CPG: HUS)

options.text: IV fluid resuscitation with isotonic crystalloid for rehydration
options.rationale: Careful IV fluid management is essential in HUS. Early volume expansion may reduce the severity of renal injury. However, fluid must be carefully titrated in the setting of oliguria and hypertension to avoid fluid overload. Isotonic crystalloid is appropriate for initial resuscitation. (Source: RCH CPG: HUS)

options.text: Antibiotic therapy targeting the Shiga toxin-producing E. coli
options.rationale: Antibiotics are specifically contraindicated in Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC) infection complicated by or at risk of HUS. Antibiotic-mediated bacterial lysis releases additional Shiga toxin, which may worsen the thrombotic microangiopathy and increase the risk of progression to HUS or worsening of established HUS. This is one of the few infections where antibiotics are actively harmful. (Source: RCH CPG: HUS)

options.text: Renal replacement therapy if oliguria persists or K+ rises
options.rationale: Renal replacement therapy (dialysis) is indicated in HUS for severe or refractory AKI with complications such as refractory hyperkalaemia, fluid overload, or uraemic encephalopathy. It is an important part of supportive management and should not be avoided. Approximately 50-70% of children with STEC-HUS require dialysis during the acute phase. (Source: RCH CPG: HUS)

explanation.summary: Typical (STEC-associated) haemolytic uraemic syndrome is the most common cause of acute kidney injury in young children. It follows diarrhoeal illness caused by Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, most commonly O157:H7. The triad is microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury. Antibiotics are specifically contraindicated as they increase Shiga toxin release and may worsen the disease. Management is supportive with careful fluid balance, blood transfusion as needed, and dialysis for severe AKI.
key_points: Antibiotics are contraindicated in STEC infection - they increase Shiga toxin release and may worsen HUS
The classic triad is microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and AKI
Schistocytes on blood film confirm microangiopathic haemolysis
Platelet transfusion is relatively contraindicated as it may fuel the thrombotic microangiopathy
50-70% of children with STEC-HUS require dialysis during the acute phase
explanation.pearls: Antibiotic administration during STEC infection increases the risk of developing HUS by 14-17 fold - the SOS response triggered by antibiotics (especially fluoroquinolones and trimethoprim) upregulates Shiga toxin production and release from dying bacteria.

stem: A 5-week-old first-born male infant presents with a 10-day history of progressively forceful, non-bilious vomiting that now occurs after every feed. His mother describes the vomit as projectile. He is hungry immediately after vomiting. He has lost 200 g from his 2-week weight check. On examination he is mildly dehydrated with a sunken fontanelle. A firm olive-shaped mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant during a test feed. Ultrasound confirms pyloric stenosis with a pyloric muscle thickness of 5 mm and channel length of 18 mm.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 160, RR 42, SpO2 99% RA, Temp 36.8, Weight 3.6 kg
data_table.Investigations: VBG: pH 7.52, pCO2 48 mmHg, HCO3 38 mmol/L, K+ 2.8 mmol/L, Na+ 133 mmol/L, Cl- 82 mmol/L (ref 98-106)

lead_in: What must be corrected before surgical intervention?

options.text: The metabolic acidosis, to reduce anaesthetic cardiac risk
options.rationale: This infant has a metabolic alkalosis (pH 7.52, HCO3 38), not acidosis. The elevated pCO2 represents respiratory compensation (hypoventilation to retain CO2). Pyloric stenosis causes loss of gastric hydrochloric acid through vomiting, producing hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Identifying the correct acid-base disturbance is essential for pre-operative correction. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

options.text: The thrombocytopenia, to reduce the risk of surgical bleeding
options.rationale: The blood results do not show thrombocytopenia. This is a distractor - pyloric stenosis does not cause thrombocytopenia. The key pre-operative concern is the metabolic alkalosis with hypokalaemia and hypochloraemia, which must be corrected with IV 0.9% NaCl with KCl supplementation before safe anaesthesia. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

options.text: The hypernatraemia, to prevent intraoperative seizures
options.rationale: The sodium is 133 mmol/L, which is low-normal to mildly hyponatraemic, not hypernatraemic. Pyloric stenosis typically causes hyponatraemia from volume depletion and aldosterone-mediated sodium retention being overwhelmed by losses. The key correction needed is the metabolic alkalosis, hypochloraemia, and hypokalaemia. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

options.text: The hypoglycaemia, to provide adequate energy for healing
options.rationale: While infants with pyloric stenosis can develop hypoglycaemia from poor oral intake, the investigations provided do not include a BSL result indicating hypoglycaemia. The critical pre-operative correction in pyloric stenosis is the electrolyte and acid-base disturbance - specifically the hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

options.text: The hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with IV fluids
options.rationale: Pyloric stenosis causes loss of gastric HCl, producing hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. This must be corrected before anaesthesia because alkalosis shifts the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve leftward (impairing tissue oxygen delivery), hypokalaemia predisposes to cardiac arrhythmias under anaesthesia, and compensatory hypoventilation may cause apnoea during induction. Correction is achieved with IV 0.9% NaCl plus KCl supplementation over 24-48 hours. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

explanation.summary: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis classically presents in first-born males at 3-6 weeks with progressive projectile non-bilious vomiting. The pathognomonic metabolic derangement is hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis from gastric acid loss. Pyloromyotomy is curative but is never an emergency - the metabolic abnormalities must be corrected first. IV 0.9% NaCl with potassium supplementation is the resuscitation fluid of choice. Surgery should only proceed once chloride exceeds 100 mmol/L and bicarbonate is below 26 mmol/L.
key_points: Pyloric stenosis causes hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis from HCl loss in vomit
Pyloromyotomy is not an emergency - correct the metabolic derangement before surgery
IV 0.9% NaCl with KCl is the resuscitation fluid - replaces chloride and potassium
Surgical readiness targets: chloride >100 mmol/L, bicarbonate <26 mmol/L, potassium >3.5 mmol/L
Respiratory compensation for metabolic alkalosis is hypoventilation - which risks apnoea under anaesthesia
explanation.pearls: The kidneys initially compensate for the alkalosis by excreting bicarbonate in urine (alkaline urine), but as volume depletion worsens, the kidneys prioritise sodium reabsorption over acid-base correction, producing the paradoxical aciduria of pyloric stenosis.

subtopic_detail: Acute cerebellar ataxia vs posterior fossa tumour
stem: A 3-year-old boy presents with a 2-day history of progressive unsteadiness and frequent falls. He had chickenpox (varicella) 10 days ago that has resolved. His parents report he was walking normally before this. On examination he has truncal ataxia, wide-based gait, and bilateral dysmetria. His speech is normal and there is no nystagmus. He is afebrile, alert, and interactive. There is no papilloedema on fundoscopy. He has no headache or vomiting.
